name: Ahi-ezer
title: Chieftain of the tribe of Dan during the wilderness journey
summary: Ahiher, son of Ammishaddai, was the tribal leader (nasi) of Dan during the Israelites' wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. God himself appointed him to assist Moses in the census and the overall organization of Israel's camp. As commander of the northern division of the camp, which also included Asher and Naphtali under his authority, he was responsible for the unit that formed the rear guard during the people's march through the wilderness—a position of significant military-strategic importance. On the eleventh day of the dedication ceremonies, Ahiher brought his offering before the altar of the tabernacle, equal to the offerings of the other tribal leaders, as an expression of the tribe of Dan's devotion to the Lord and its equal standing among Israel's twelve tribes.
relatedPersons: Netanel son of Zuar, leader from the tribe of Issachar
Eliab son of Helon, leader from the tribe of Zebulun

keyEvents.title: Appointed as Leader of Dan
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer was appointed by God as leader and representative of the tribe of Dan to stand beside Moses during the organization of the people.

keyEvents.title: The Census in the Wilderness
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer participated in the census of Israelite men aged twenty years and older. The tribe of Dan was counted at 62,700 fighting men.

keyEvents.title: Camp Arrangement North of the Tabernacle
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer led Dan's division, which was positioned on the north side of the tabernacle along with the tribes of Asher and Naphtali. This division formed the last group to break camp during the march.

keyEvents.title: Offering at the Dedication of the Altar
keyEvents.description: On the eleventh day, Ahiezer brought his offering at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar, including a silver plate, a silver bowl, a gold bowl with incense, as well as burnt offerings and sin offerings.

keyEvents.title: Leader of the Rear Guard at Departure
keyEvents.description: When the Israelites broke camp, Ahiezer led the rear guard with Dan's military division as the last unit in the marching order.

versions.summary: Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, was the chosen leader of the tribe of Dan during the Israelites' wilderness journey. He was appointed by God to assist Moses with the census and the organization of Israel's camp. He also brought his offering at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar.
versions.title: Leader of the Tribe of Dan
versions.reason: [minor] Ahiezer had more roles than just 'leader'. He was also a tribal chief and military commander. It may be useful to add more specific roles such as 'tribal chieftain' and 'army leader'.; [minor] The summary is good, but could be expanded slightly to mention his role as leader of the rear guard during the march, which shows his military significance.; [minor] Verses 27-28-29-30 concern Asher and Naphtali, not only Dan. Ahiezer's specific role as leader of the camp of Dan (north side) is mentioned primarily in verse 25. Nevertheless, verses 25-31 are reasonable to include for the entire section.; [minor] Numbers 10:25 refers to the camp/banner of Dan breaking camp, and verse 25 mentions Ahiezer specifically. Verses 26-27 mention the leaders of Asher (Pagiel) and Naphtali (Akira), not Ahiezer directly. It is not wrong to include them for context, but strictly speaking only verse 25 concerns Ahiezer.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. Information should be added about the meaning of the name, historical context regarding the role of tribal chieftains, and the placement of the tribe of Dan in the camp.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1500 BC' is one possible dating of the Exodus. A broader dating such as 'c. 1400s BC' or 'c. 1500–1400 BC' would be more accurate given various chronological views. Alternatively, one could keep the current formulation as an approximation.

versions.reason: [minor] The word 'theophant' is incorrect. The correct technical term is 'theophoric' (a name that carries a divine name). Furthermore, it is debatable whether Ahiezer is a theophoric name – it means "my brother is help," and "brother" does not necessarily refer to God but could refer to a relative. The phrasing should be adjusted.; [minor] 'participated' is more correctly written as 'participated' (which is correct), but the phrasing "participated in the census of Israelite men over twenty years old" is somewhat awkward. Better: "participated in the census of Israelite men from twenty years and upward."; [minor] The phrasing "the northern camp division" is correct, but the connection between the camp arrangement and the rear-guard role could have been expressed more clearly to avoid giving the impression that these are two separate matters.; [major] Numbers 10:25 mentions that the Danite camp broke camp, but the verse specifically names the commander. Verse 25 alone does not cover the entire context – verses 25–26 provide a more complete picture, where Ahiezer is mentioned in verse 25 as the leader of the military division of the tribe of Dan.

versions.summary: Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, served as the leader of the tribe of Dan during the Israelites' wilderness journey. He was appointed by God to stand beside Moses during the census and organization of Israel's camp. In the camp arrangement, he led the northern division, which also included Asher and Naphtali. This positioning meant that his division formed the rear guard when the people broke camp and marched – a militarily important task. On the eleventh of twelve consecration days, Ahiezer brought his offering to the altar of the tabernacle, an expression of the tribe of Dan's devotion and equality among Israel's twelve tribes.

A slightly broader formulation such as "c. 1400s BC" could have been more neutral, but this is acceptable given the uncertainty.; [minor] The verb "deltok" should be written "deltok" (correct) or alternatively "was with". This is correct Norwegian; no change needed. (Check: actually "deltok" is correct.); [minor] The summary is good and informative, but the phrasing "formed the rear guard when the people broke camp and were on the march" could be tightened slightly for even better flow. It should also be clarified that he led the northern camp/division, which is already included. The summary is solid but can be polished marginally to distinguish it from earlier versions.; [minor] The footnote about nesi'im has the source "theological", but the content deals as much with social/historical organization. "Historical" could have been more appropriate, but "theological" is also defensible since it concerns leadership structure in God's people.

footnotes.text: The name Ahi-ezer (Hebrew: אֲחִיעֶזֶר, 'Achi'ezer') means 'my brother is help' or 'brother's helper'. The name expresses trust in kinship solidarity and support, and it is debated whether 'brother' here refers to God or a human relative.

The name Ammishaddai (Hebrew: עַמִּישַׁדָּי) means 'my people are the Almighty' or 'Shaddai is my kinsman'. This links the family name to the ancient divine name El Shaddai, which was especially associated with the patriarchal era.

The tribe of Dan was positioned on the north side of the tabernacle together with Asher and Naphtali, forming the last division to break camp during the march. This rear position had military-strategic significance as a rearguard and protection for the rest of the camp.

The tribal leaders (Hebrew: nesi'im, נְשִׂיאִים) mentioned in Numbers served a dual role as both civil leaders and military commanders. They represented their tribes in all official contexts and acted as a link between Moses and the people.

The fact that each tribal leader brought identical offerings at the dedication of the altar (Num 7) underscores the equality of the tribes before God, even though the gifts were given on different days. Ahi-ezer's day was the eleventh, second to last of the twelve tribes.

The camp arrangement described in Numbers 2 reflects a structured military and cultic organization of the people around the tabernacle. The fourfold division (east, south, west, north) with three tribes in each section has parallels to other ancient Near Eastern camp arrangements known from Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources.
